Appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County. 
Honorable Marian E. Perkins, Judge, Presiding. 
No. 2020 CH 01473 

PRESIDING JUSTICE QUISH delivered the judgment of the court. 
Presiding Justice Lyle and Justice Navarro concurred in the judgment. 
ORDER 
¶ 1 Held: Service on a voluntary unincorporated association by publication was proper under 
735 ILCS 5/2-205.1. 

¶ 2 After the circuit court entered a mortgage foreclosure judgment in favor of plaintiff 
Nationstar Mortgage LLC, d/b/a Mr. Cooper (“Nationstar”), and confirmed a subsequent judicial 
sale of the property at issue, defendant Infinite Light, a voluntary unincorporated association 
(“Infinite Light”), appeared and filed a motion to quash service, contesting Nationstar’s service on 

- 2 - 
Infinite Light by publication. Following an evidentiary hearing on the motion to quash, the circuit 
court denied Infinite Light’s motion, finding no defects in Nationstar’s service of Infinite Light by 
publication. For the following reasons, we affirm. 
¶ 3 On February 4, 2020, Nationstar filed a complaint to foreclose on a mortgage securing real 
property at 7236 South Michigan Avenue in Chicago (“the Property”). Defendant Simeon Lewis, 
who previously owned the Property before deeding it to Infinite Light, was served by substitute 
service on February 6, 2020. On February 26, 2020, Nationstar filed an affidavit for service by 
publication under section 2- 206 of the Code of Civil Procedure (“Code”) (735 ILCS 5/2-206) 
(West 2020)), in which its attorney, Randal Berg, averred that the last known address for Infinite 
Light, an unincorporated association, was P.O. Box 198891 in Chicago and that appropriate 
representatives of Infinite Light or its place of residence could not be located. Berg also stated that 
an affidavit of due diligence was attached, but no such attachment appears in the record. 
¶ 4 An affidavit of due diligence executed by Stephan Jenkins of ProVest Services LLC, dated 
February 13, 2020, was later attached as an exhibit to Nationstar’s October 18, 2021, motion for 
judgment against Infinite Light. Jenkins averred that he was unable to discover Infinite Light’s 
place of residence af ter performing a diligent inquiry that consisted of searching a telephone 
directory and searching a national secretary of state database, and he made “other inquiries” 
revealing no listings for registered agents, registered officers, or a corporate property address. On 
March 16, 2020, Nationstar filed a Certificate of Publication reflecting that notice of the action 
had been published in the Chicago Daily Law Bulletin on February 28, March 6, and March 13, 
2020. A copy of a postcard mailed from the Clerk of the Circuit Court to Infinite Light at P.O. Box 
198891, which contained a return- to-sender stamp stating, “Attempted – Not Known, Unable to 
Forward,” was filed April 3, 2020. 

- 3 - 
¶ 5 Lewis appeared and participated in the lawsuit. He initially filed a motion to quash service 
on him, which was denied. The circuit court later granted Nationstar’s motion for summary 
judgment against Lewis and entered a judgment of foreclosure against him on January 28, 2022. 
Lewis appealed. In Nationstar Mortgage LLC v. Lewis , 2026 IL App (1st) 250466-U, this court 
affirmed. The Illinois Supreme Court denied Lewis’ petition for leave to appeal on September 30, 
2026. 
¶ 6 Meanwhile, the circuit court also entered judgment against Infinite Light and a judicial sale 
was conducted in June 2022. Nationstar was the successful bidder. The court confirmed the sale 
on November 2, 2023. 
¶ 7 Also on November 2, 2023, counsel for Infinite Light filed his appearance. On November 
15, 2023, Infinite Light filed a motion to quash service of process, arguing that Nationstar’s service 
by publication was insufficient because its affidavit merely recited statutory language without 
providing additional detail, Jenkins’ due diligence affidavit could not be used to support the 
affidavit for service by publication because it was only filed later with Nationstar’s motion for 
judgment, and Nationstar did not conduct a diligent inquiry . Infinite Light cited affidavits from 
two residents of the Property averring that no process server ever contacted them about Infinite 
Light or this lawsuit and no notices were posted at the Property. 
¶ 8 In response, Nationstar argued that its affidavits satisfied statutory requirements and that 
service by publication was the only possible method of service because Infinite Light had no office, 
street address, or publicly available documents identifying any officers or agents. Nationstar 
asserted that the only publicly available document regarding Infinite Light was the quitclaim deed 
transferring the Property from Lewis to Infinite Light, but that document did not identify Infinite 
Light’s street address, officers, or agents. The deed was attached to Nationstar’s response, and it 

- 4 - 
contains Lewis ’ signature as the seller/grantor. Accompanying the deed was a Statement by 
Grantor and Grantee. The signature line for “Grantee or Agent” was signed “Infinite Light,” and 
Infinite Light’s grantee statement was sworn to by Lewis. In its reply, Infinite Light argued t hat 
Lewis’ signature swearing to the grantee’s statement was evidence that Lewis was an agent of 
Infinite Light and thus, Nationstar was required to attempt personal service on Lewis before 
resorting to service by publication. 
¶ 9 After the parties completed discovery, the court found a material issue of fact and held an 
evidentiary hearing on the motion to quash. No transcript of the hearing appears in the record, but 
the court set forth some of the testimony in its ruling . In particular, the court recounted that Ben 
Baldwin, a manager at ProVest, testified that Stephan Jenkins was no longer employed at ProVest, 
but he had personal knowledge of Jenkins’ work. Baldwin testified that “there were no listings for 
Infinite Light, An Unincorporated Association through the Secretary of State website, telephone 
company, nor any listed Registered Agents or Registered Officers.” Baldwin also confirmed that 
Infinite Light’s quitclaim deed listed its address as P.O. Box 198891. The court further recounted 
that Randal Berg, Nationstar’s attorney, testified that the quitclaim deed conveyed the Property 
from Lewis to Infinite Light and that Lewis “signed upon the line designated for the ‘Grantor’ [sic] 
or ‘Agent.’” 
¶ 10 Following the evidentiary hearing, the court found that, under section 2-205.1 of the Code 
(735 ILCS 5/2- 205.1 (West 2020)), which governs the service of process on voluntary 
unincorporated associations, it was legally appropriate and sufficient for Nationstar to elect to 
serve Infinite Light by publication. Further, the court found that Jenkins “executed due diligence 
in his search for Infinite Light” and only discovered P.O. Box 198891, which was neither an office 
address nor an address of any officer of the association. The court also found that Nationstar was 

- 5 - 
unable to personally serve an officer of Infinite Light because none w as registered with the 
Secretary of State and Nationstar could not have served an agent at Infinite Light’s office because 
no agent was registered. Similarly, the court rejected Infinite Light’s argument that Lewis’ 
signature on the grantee statement attached to the quitclaim deed established that he should be 
recognized as a registered agent, finding that a registered agent is normally on record with the 
Secretary of State, which Lewis was not. The court ultimately denied Infinite Light’s motion to 
quash, finding that Infinite Light did not meet its burden and Nationstar’s affidavits and service by 
publication complied with the statutory requirements and were not defective . Infinite Light 
appeals. 
¶ 11 The sole issue in this appeal is whether Nationstar could serve Infinite Light, a voluntary 
unincorporated association, by publication under section 2-205.1 of the Code. To enter a valid 
judgment, the circuit court must have jurisdiction over both the subject matter and the parties. BAC 
Home Loans Servicing, LP v. Mitchell , 2014 IL 116311, ¶ 17. The failure to effect service of 
process deprives the court of jurisdiction over the defendant and renders a subsequent default 
judgment void. Bank of New York Mellon v. Karbowski, 2014 IL App (1st) 130112, ¶ 12. 
¶ 12 When a motion to quash service of process is filed more than 30 days after a judgment, as 
Infinite Light’s motion was in this case, it is construed as a petition to vacate a void judgment 
under section 2-1401 of the Code (735 ILCS 5/2- 1401 (West 2022)). See OneWest Bank, FSB v. 
Topor, 2013 IL App (1st) 120010, ¶¶ 14-15. Because the court held an evidentiary hearing on 
Infinite Light’s motion, we employ a mixed standard of review. See Department of Healthcare & 
Family Services ex rel. Sanders v. Edwards, 2022 IL App (1st) 210409, ¶ 44. We review the court’s 
findings of fact deferentially under the manifest weight of the evidence standard, reversing “‘only 
when the opposite conclusion is clearly evident or where the factual findings upon which it is based 

- 6 - 
are unreasonable, arbitrary, or not based on the evidence.’” Id. (quoting 1350 Lake Shore 
Associates v. Randall, 401 Ill. App. 3d 96, 102 (2010)). Meanwhile, we apply de novo review to 
the court’s legal conclusions. Id. 
¶ 13 The service of process on a voluntary unincorporated association is governed by section 
2-205.1, which sets forth three options for a plaintiff: 
“A voluntary unincorporated association sued in its own name may be served by leaving a 
copy of the process with any officer of the association personally or by leaving a copy of 
the process at the office of the association with an agent of the association . A voluntary 
unincorporated association sued in its own name may also be notified by publication and 
mail in like manner and with like effect as individuals.” 735 ILCS 5/2-205.1. 
¶ 14 Regarding publication, section 2-206(a- 5) of the Code (735 ILCS 5/2-206(a- 5) (West 
2020)) provides, in relevant part, that , in a mortgage foreclosure action, service may be 
accomplished through publication when the plaintiff files “an affidavit showing that the defendant 
*** on due inquiry cannot be found, *** so that process cannot be served upon him or her, and 
stating the place of residence of the defendant , if known, or that upon diligent inquiry his or her 
place of residence cannot be ascertained.” 
¶ 15 Infinite Light argues only that Nationstar was required to attempt service on Infinite Light 
through its agent, Lewis, before it could serve by publication under section 2-205.1, and thus, 
because Nationstar did not do so, service by publication was inappropriate. Nationstar responds 
that service by publication was proper because its affidavits demonstrated compliance with 
statutory due diligence requirements and Infinite Light failed to show that it could have discovered 
an officer who could have been personally served or an office where service could have been made 

- 7 - 
upon an agent. We agree with Nationstar that service by publication was appropriate in this case 
and the court properly denied Infinite Light’s motion to quash. 
¶ 16 The plain language of

leads.caseName: SUN BRITE SERVICES, INC. v. KRISTINA GUTIERREZ
leads.text:
FOURTH DIVISION
MCFADDEN, P. J.,
WATKINS and PADGETT, JJ.
NOTICE: Motions for reconsideration must be
received no later than 4:30 pm on the 10th day after
the decision was issued to be deemed timely filed. 
https://www.gaappeals.gov/rules
October 28, 2026
In the Court of Appeals of Georgia
A26A0912. SUN BRITE SERVICES, INC. v. GUTIERREZ et al.
MCFADDEN, Presiding Judge.
Norbert Goodrum, an employee of appellant Sun Brite Services, Inc., struck
and killed a pedestrian while he was driving his personal car. Kristina Gutierrez, the
mother of the pedestrian’s child, and Hillary B. Cranford1, the administrator of his
estate (together, “the plaintiffs”), filed this lawsuit against Goodrum and Sun Brite,
alleging that Sun Brite was vicariously liable for Goodrum’s negligence because
Goodrum was acting in the course and scope of his employment at the time of the fatal
collision. 
1 In the record, Cranford’s first name is spelled as both “Hilary” and
“Hillary.” 
Sun Brite appeals from two interlocutory orders: an order imposing spoliation
sanctions and an order denying its motion for summary judgment. At the hearing on
those motions, the parties argued but did not present evidence. Consequently, the
summary judgment standard for disputes of fact obtained as to both motions. The trial
court did not employ that standard on the spoliation issue. So we vacate the trial
court’s order granting the plaintiffs’ motion for spoliation sanctions. In light of this
holding, we also vacate the order denying Sun Brite’s motion for summary judgment.
We remand the case for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion.2 
1. Background
Sun Brite is a commercial and industrial pressure washing company. Jeff
Robison is Sun Brite’s sole owner and CEO, and Goodrum is an employee. 
At the time of the fatal collision, Sun Brite employees drove their personal cars
to the Sun Brite facility; picked up their assigned, printed work order from a job board
at the office; and then retrieved the equipment needed to complete the job, including
a company-owned truck equipped with a pressure washer, which they would drive to
2 Oral argument was held in this case on April 28, 2026, and is archived on the
court’s website. See Court of Appeals of Georgia, Oral Argument, Case No.
A26A0912 (April 28, 2026), available at https://vimeo.com/1188466885.
2
the job site. Sun Brite employees communicated internally using Slack, “a cloud-based
team communication platform.” https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slack_(software)
(retrieved September 16, 2026), and by text messages and telephone calls. 
 Some of Sun Brite’s clients are shopping centers, which must be cleaned when
they are closed at night, so Robison allows his employees flexibility in their hours; as
long as his employees complete the job by 6 or 7 in the morning, they may begin the
work when they prefer. 
Goodrum worked as a senior technician for Sun Brite. He was a night-shift
employee, but some evidence showed that some days in the weeks before the collision,
he began work earlier than the typical night-shift start time of between 9 p.m. and 10
p.m. If a particular job allowed Goodrum to begin work earlier than ususal, Robinson
would inform him by text message or phone call. 
On the night of the fatal collision, October 25, 2021, Goodrum was driving his
personal car from his residence to the Sun Brite facility in order to pick up a pressure-
washing truck to use at a job site. He was wearing a Sun Brite uniform and had a safety
vest in a backpack in his car. He did not see the pedestrian in the road, and struck him,
killing him. 
3
On December 17, 2021, Gutierrez sent Sun Brite a letter, requesting that it 
maintain all records relating to the injuries and death of [the pedestrian].
This request includes all communications with Norbert Goodrum and all
scheduling documents for Norbert Goodrum’s employment for the two
weeks before and after this collision, all photographs, videos, reports,
and any other documentation relating to this collision, and Norbert
Goodrum’s employment status on the date of the collision. 
After the plaintiffs filed this lawsuit, Sun Brite filed a motion for summary
judgment and the plaintiffs filed a motion for spoliation sanctions. The trial court held
a hearing on the motions, at which the parties argued but did not present evidence,
and then entered an order denying Sun Brite’s motion for summary judgment and
granting the plaintiffs’ motion for spoliation sanctions. We granted Sun Brite’s
application for interlocutory appeal, and this appeal followed. 
2. Spoliation
“Spoliation refers to the destruction or failure to preserve evidence that is
necessary to contemplated or pending litigation. AMLI Residential Properties v. Ga.
Power Co., 293 Ga. App. 358, 361 (1) (667 SE2d 150) (2008) (citation modified). See
also OCGA § 24-14-22. Generally, the trial court 
4
has wide discretion in adjudicating spoliation issues, and such discretion
will not be disturbed absent abuse. Where a trial court makes findings of
fact in ruling on a spoliation claim, this [c]ourt will uphold those findings
if there is any evidence to support them, i.e., unless they are clearly
erroneous. When the trial court imposes a sanction that is inconsistent
with its factual findings, the trial court abuses its discretion.
Cowan Systems v. Collier, 361 Ga. App. 823, 823-824 (865 SE2d 619) (2021) (citation
modified). 
But here, there has not been an evidentiary hearing. So the trial court was
required to construe the evidence “under the standard applicable to a motion for
summary judgment, and as the part[y] opposing the motion, [Sun Brite is] entitled to
have the evidence in the record viewed in the light most favorable to [it] and to have
all reasonable inferences from the evidence drawn in [its] favor.” UPS of Am. v.
Whitlock, 366 Ga. App. 542, 555(2)(a) (883 SE2d 556) (2023) (citation modified).
Absent an evidentiary hearing, the court may not decide credibility issues. Id. at 556-
57(2)(a)(i). 
Sun Brite argues that the trial court applied the wrong legal standard when it
found that spoliation had occurred. We agree.
5
We begin by identifying the evidence plaintiffs claimed they had asked Sun Brite
to preserve but that it had not preserved. About that the plaintiffs were not precise.
See Cowan Systems, 361 Ga. App. at 825 n.2 (reviewing motion for sanctions to
determine what evidence the movant alleged was spoliated); Whitlock, 366 Ga. App.
at 555(2)(a) (“the way in which the plaintiff[ ] raised ... the spoliation claim[ ] against
the defendant[ ] is important to our review of the issue before us”). At one point in
the motion, the plaintiffs alleged that Sun Brite failed to preserve its
“communications” with Goodrum, without defining what they meant by
“communications.” At another point they alleged specifically that Sun Brite had not
preserved text messages and records of telephone calls between Sun Brite employees
and Goodrum “in the week leading up to the collision.” They also alleged that Sun
Brite failed to preserve communications with Goodrum “in the two weeks leading up
to” the collision. They elsewhere focused on Sun Brite’s communications with
Goodrum while he was driving to work on the night of the fatal collision and the calls
and text massages “in the hours leading up to the collision.” As to all of these
communications, however, the plaintiffs alleged that Sun Brite failed to preserve the
evidence because Robison replaced his cellular telephone, an undisputed fact. 
6
From this we conclude that in their motion the plaintiffs contended that the
evidence they requested Sun Brite to retain but that Sun Brite did not preserve is the
text messages and records of telephone calls between Goodrum and Robison as
reflected on Robison’s replaced cellular telephone in the two weeks leading up to the
collision and on the date of the collision itself, or from October 11, 2021, through
October 25, 2021.3 
The trial court found as fact, see In re Estate of Flournoy, 373 Ga. App. 133,
138(2) (907 SE2d 724) (2024), that Sun Brite “spoliated the requested records,”
without specifying which particular records. So we must conclude that the trial court
found that Sun Brite spoliated the “requested records” described above: the text
messages and records of telephone calls between Goodrum and Robison, as reflected
on Robison’s replaced telephone, in the two weeks leading up to the collision and on
the date of the collision itself. 
3 In their appellees’ brief, the plaintiffs also argue about Sun Brite’s failure to
preserve Goodrum’s cellular telephone, Slack messages, and work orders. But they
did not make these arguments in their motion for spoliation sanctions, so these
categories of evidence were not before the trial court when he ruled on the spoliation
sanctions motion.
7
We hold that the evidence supports the trial court’s factual finding of spoliation
only in part. Even when viewing the evidence in Sun Brite’s favor, as the trial court
was required to do given the procedural posture of this case, the evidence is
undisputed that Sun Brite failed to preserve text messages and records of telephone
calls between Goodrum and Robison, as documented on Robison’s replaced
telephone, for the period of October 11, 2021, through October 24, 2021. Robison
testified in his deposition that he and Goodrum would have communicated, including
about job start times, by text message or telephone call in this time period. 
But when viewed in Sun Brite’s favor, the evidence does not suppport a finding
that Sun Brite failed to preserve text messages and records of telephone calls between
Goodrum and Robison on the day of the fatal collision, at least before the collision
occurred.4 Goodrum testified in his deposition that on that day, he did not speak or
text with anyone from Sun Brite before the collision occurred. Robison also testified
in his deposition that he would not have communicated with Goodrum on that day
before the collision occurred. And although Robison also testified in his deposition
4 The evidence is undisputed that Goodrum and Robison communicated by
telephone shortly after the collision, but the plaintiffs did not argue about post-
collision communications in their sanctions motion. 
8
that, most likely, that day Goodrum would have received a text message or a phone
call from him or the operations manager informing him what time to begin work, he
clarified that such information “could have been communicated days before in a
conversation.” The trial court could not make a credibility determination, since it did
not hold an evidentiary hearing, and was required to view this testimony in the light
most favorable to Sun Brite. Properly viewed, the evidence does not show that there
were text messages and records of telephone calls between Goodrum and Robison on
the day of the fatal collision before the collision occurred. “It is axiomatic that in order
for there to be spoliation, the evidence in question must have existed. ...” Sentry Select
Ins. Co. v. Treadwell, 318 Ga. App. 844, 847(2)(c) (734 SE2d 818) (2012). So when
viewed in favor of Sun Brite, the evidence does not support the trial court’s factual
finding that Sun Brite spoliated text messages and records of telephone calls between
Goodrum and Robison on the day of the fatal collision before the collision occurred. 
(b) Sanction
Once the trial court has determined that spoliation occurred, the court should
weigh five factors to determine an appropriate sanction: 
(1) whether the party seeking sanctions was prejudiced as a result of the
destroyed evidence; (2) whether the prejudice could be cured; (3) the
9
practical importance of the evidence; (4) whether the destroying party
acted in good or bad faith; and (5) the potential for abuse if any expert
testimony about the destroyed evidence was not excluded.5
Whitlock, 366 Ga. App. at 555(2)(a) (citation modified). “[W]e will not disturb a trial
court’s imposition of sanc
