leads.caseName: Gre Downtowner Llc, D/b/a Addison On Fourth, V. City Of Seattle
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON

 GRE DOWNTOWNER LLC, a
 Washington limited liability company, No. 87886-7-I
 d/b/a ADDISON ON FOURTH,
 DIVISION ONE
 Appellant,
 PUBLISHED OPINION
 v.

 CITY OF SEATTLE,

 Respondent.

 MANN, J. — GRE Downtowner LLC (GRE Downtowner) is a real estate company

that operates Addison on Fourth (Addison), a low-income apartment complex in the City

of Seattle (City). In 2024, GRE Downtowner sued the City alleging inverse

condemnation claims for partial and per se regulatory takings stemming from the

collective impact of a series of rental housing ordinances. GRE Downtowner appeals

the trial court’s order dismissing its claims under CR 12(b)(6). Because we conclude

that GRE Downtowner pleaded sufficient facts to support its claims, we reverse.

 I. FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND

 The Addison is a low-income housing complex located near the City’s downtown

area. In 2012, GRE Downtowner purchased the Addison for $12.5 million and invested
 No. 87886-7-I/2

an additional $26.5 million to qualify for the federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit

(LIHTC) program. 1

 The LIHTC program was created to incentivize private developers to invest in

and maintain affordable housing by offering a 10-year annual tax credit in exchange for

restricting rents and reserving units for low-income tenants over a 30-year period. It is

currently considered the most important resource for creating affordable housing in the

United States. In Washington, the LIHTC program is administered by the Washington

State Housing and Finance Commission (Commission), which is responsible for

creating the plan and the policies for the fair allocation of the tax credit to housing

projects. In awarding tax credits to GRE Downtowner, the Commission provided bond

financing for the acquisition and redevelopment of the Addison.

 While understanding that sustainably running low-income housing can be

challenging, GRE Downtowner considered its financial projections for the Addison

reasonable based on its considerable institutional experience in developing housing

projects, as well as working with federal, state, and municipal housing and landlord-

tenant regulations. Confidence in the financial projections for the Addison was shared

by several entities: the Commission; Citigroup as bond underwriter; Freddie Mac as

credit enhancer for the bonds issued by the Commission to finance the project; East

West Bank as credit enhancer for the bonds issued during the construction and

 1 The LIHTC gives state and local LIHTC-allocating agencies approximately $12 billion annually

to issue tax credits for the acquisition, rehabilitation, or new construction of rental housing targeted to
lower-income households. Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) Program, U.S. DEP’T OF HOUS. &
URB. DEV. OFF. OF POL’Y DEV. AND RSCH. (PD&R), https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/lihtc.html (last
visited Oct. 5, 2026).

 -2-
 No. 87886-7-I/3

renovation of the Addison; and Stratford Downtowner LP as LIHTC investor

(collectively, stakeholders).

 The Addison was placed in service under the LIHTC program in 2013 and was

fully renovated and operationally stable by 2015. It provides 254 studio and one-

bedroom apartments for City residents earning 60 percent of the area’s median income,

including set-asides for residents with disabilities, 46 artist studios, and four commercial

spaces. The maximum monthly rent for studio and one-bedroom apartments is set

annually by the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)

based on the City’s median income. For instance, based on a one-person median

income of $54,360 in 2022, HUD set the Addison’s maximum monthly rent at $1,358 for

a studio unit and $1,455 for a one-bedroom unit.

 From 2015 through 2018, the annual net cash flow stemming from the Addison

remained positive, with GRE Downtowner collecting 90.6 percent, 93.4 percent, 93.7

percent, and 93.9 percent of the Addison’s maximum annual rental income,

respectively. Starting in 2018, however, the Seattle City Council (City Council) adopted

a series of ordinances and a resolution aimed at increasing access to affordable

housing (collectively, the City ordinances). Beginning in 2019, GRE Downtowner began

experiencing changes in the Addison’s occupancy levels. The collection of maximum

annual rental income dropped from 87 percent in 2019 to 73.3 percent in 2020, 69.2

percent in 2021, 56.1 percent in 2022, and 44.1 percent in 2023. In addition, bad

debt—unrealized rent unlikely to be recovered from the resident—surged. So did

expenses related to security, maintenance, administration, marketing, and insurance.

According to GRE Downtowner, the City ordinances made the sustainable operation of

 -3-
 No. 87886-7-I/4

the Addison impossible because they fundamentally altered its economic relationship

with tenants and nontenants. From having a positive annual net cash flow, the Addison

lost $683,353 in 2020; $980,043 in 2021; $1.8 million in 2022; and $2.7 million in 2023.

 On January 16, 2018, the City Council passed the Fair Chance Housing

Ordinance (FCHO). Ordinance 125515. The FCHO prevents landlords from denying

tenancy or evicting an existing tenant based on their criminal history. SEATTLE

MUNICIPAL CODE (SMC) 14.09.025(A).

 On September 30, 2019, the City Council passed the Roommate Ordinance.

Ordinance 125950. The Roommate Ordinance bestows occupancy rights to “a tenant’s

immediate family, an additional resident who is not a member of the tenant’s immediate

family, and the additional resident’s immediate family.” SMC 7.24.030(I)(1). The

definition of “immediately family” under the Roommate Ordinance includes a broad

variety of third parties, including family members and nonfamily members. SMC

7.24.020. The Roommate Ordinance permits a landlord to screen and deny occupancy

to the additional nonfamily resident based on the screening results, subject to the

FCHO. SMC 7.24.030(I)(5). While a tenant’s immediate family can be screened, they

may not be excluded from occupancy absent limited exceptions, such as a lifetime sex

offender registration requirement. SMC 7.24.030(I)(5), 7.24.032(A). Lastly, if a tenant

vacates the rental unit before the expiration of the lease agreement, the tenant’s

immediate family and the additional nonfamily resident may become parties to the

existing agreement. SMC 7.24.031(A)-(C).

 On February 10, 2020, the City Council passed the Winter Eviction Ban, which

precludes evictions from December 1 through March 1 based on a series of factors,

 -4-
 No. 87886-7-I/5

including evictions that are the result of nonpayment of rent. Ordinance 126041; SMC

22.206.160(C)(8). 2

 Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic—March 2020 through February 2022—the

City also maintained an additional eviction moratorium that provided a nearly complete

defense to eviction (COVID-19 Eviction Moratorium). City of Seattle Res. 31938 (March

16, 2020). The COVID-19 Eviction Moratorium applied to all instances of nonpayment

of rent without requiring a showing of inability to pay.

 On September 27, 2021, the City Council passed Ordinance 126450, which

increased the minimum notice period that landlords must provide before imposing any

rent increase on their tenants from 60 to 180 days. SMC 7.24.030(A). That same day,

the City Council also passed Ordinance 126451, the Economic Displacement

Relocation Assistance (EDRA). Ch. 22.212 SMC. EDRA requires a landlord to pay a

tenant if the landlord proposes a rent increase of 10 percent or more, causing the tenant

to vacate the housing unit. SMC 22.212.030-.070. Specifically, EDRA requires a

landlord to provide financial assistance to a tenant equivalent to the tenant’s average

new monthly rent for three months, regardless of whether the tenant suffered any

increased costs. SMC 22.212.050.

 According to GRE Downtowner, the economic effect of the City ordinances on

the Addison has been severe. From being an economic success, the Addison now

loses millions of dollars each year, with operational losses totaling nearly $6 million

 2 SMC 22.206.160(C) has since been recodified as SMC 22.205.080(A)-(C).

 -5-
 No. 87886-7-I/6

through 2023. In addition, the Addison is now functionally valueless on an income

approach appraisal basis.

 On October 22, 2024, GRE Downtowner sued the City in King County Superior

Court, alleging inverse condemnation claims for partial and per se regulatory takings

under Article I, Section 16 of the Washington Constitution. The claims stemmed from

the combined effect of the City ordinances as applied to the Addison.

 On January 17, 2025, the City moved to dismiss GRE Downtowner’s claims

under CR 12(b)(6). After hearing argument, the trial court granted the City’s motion via

oral ruling on February 14, 2025, and entered a written order reflecting the same on

February 21, 2025.

 GRE Downtowner appeals. 3

 II. DISCUSSION

 GRE Downtowner argues that the trial court erred in dismissing its inverse

condemnation claims for partial and per se regulatory takings at the CR 12(b)(6) stage.

We agree.

 A. Standard of Review

 We review a superior court’s decision on a CR 12(b)(6) motion de novo. Wash.

Food Indus. Ass’n & Maplebear, Inc. v. City of Seattle, 1 Wn.3d 1, 17, 524 P.3d 181

(2023). Dismissal is proper only if the court concludes that the plaintiff cannot prove

any set of facts consistent with the complaint that would justify recovery. Wash. Food

Indus., 1 Wn.3d at 17. The court presumes “all facts alleged in the complaint to be true

 3 On October 10, 2025, the City’s motion to transfer the appeal to the Washington Supreme Court

was denied. Comm’r’s Ruling at 4, No. 104634-1 (Wash. Oct. 10, 2025).

 -6-
 No. 87886-7-I/7

and may consider hypothetical facts supporting the plaintiff’s claims.” Wash. Food

Indus., 1 Wn.3d at 17. The focus of our analysis is “whether the plaintiff’s claim is

legally sufficient: if the plaintiff’s claim remains legally insufficient even under their

proffered hypothetical facts, dismissal is appropriate.”4 Wash. Food Indus., 1 Wn.3d at

17.

 Like its nearly identical federal counterpart, the Washington Constitution provides

that “[n]o private property shall be taken or damaged for public or private use without

just compensation having been first made.” 5 WASH. CONST. art. I, § 16; accord U.S.

CONST. amend. V. A regulation that is an otherwise valid exercise of police power may

go overboard in its impact on a property owner such that it constitutes a regulatory

taking, requiring compensation. Wash. Food Indus., 1 Wn.3d at 30. Under Washington

law, regulatory takings are characterized as either “partial” or “per se.” Wash. Food

Indus., 1 Wn.3d at 32.

 In Yim v. City of Seattle, 194 Wn.2d 651, 658-59, 451 P.3d 675 (2019),

Washington’s Supreme Court clarified that there was no Washington-specific test for a

regulatory takings analysis; rather, Washington courts follow the framework laid out by

the United States Supreme Court in Lingle v. Chevron U.S.A. Inc., 544 U.S. 528, 125,

S. Ct. 2074, 161 L. Ed. 2d 876 (2005). Chevron first recognized two categories of per

 4 Unlike its federal counterpart, Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6), Washington’s CR 12(b)(6) employs a

more lenient standard of review. In McCurry v. Chevy Chase Bank, FSB, 169 Wn.2d 96, 102, 233 P.3d
861 (2010), Washington’s Supreme Court declined to adopt the federal “plausibility” standard, which
includes “a determination of the likelihood of success on the merits, so that a trial judge can dismiss a
claim, even where the law does provide a remedy for the conduct alleged by the plaintiff, if that judge
does not believe it is plausible the claim will ultimately succeed.”
 5 The United States Constitution prohibits only the “taking” of private property for public use

without just compensation. U.S. CONST. amend. V.

 -7-

leads.text:
[Cite as Premiere Settlement & Title, L.L.C. v. Cline, 2026-Ohio-4226.] 

IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO 
ELEVENTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 
TRUMBULL COUNTY 

PREMIERE SETTLEMENT 
& TITLE, L.L.C., 

 Plaintiff-Appellee, 

 - vs - 

JAMES R. CLINE, 

 Defendant/Cross- 
 Claimant/Cross- 
 Defendant-Appellant, 

ASHLEY A. LOKASH, 

 Defendant/Cross- 
 Defendant/Cross- 
 Claimant-Appellee. 
CASE NO. 2026-T-0029 

Civil Appeal from the 
Court of Common Pleas 

Trial Court No. 2024 CV 00381 

OPINION AND JUDGMENT ENTRY 

Decided: October 26, 2026 
Judgment: Affirmed 

Damian P. DeGenova , DeGenova & Yarwood, Ltd., 42 North Phelps Street, 
Youngstown, OH 44503 (For Plaintiff-Appellee). 

Stephen A. Turner, Turner, May & Shepherd, 185 High Street, N.E., Warren, OH 44481 
(For Defendant-Appellant). 

Michael J. Fredericka , Neuman and Fredericka Law Office, L.L.C., 761 North Cedar 
Avenue, Suite 1, Niles, OH 44446 (For Defendant-Appellee). 

MATT LYNCH, P.J. 
{¶1} This appeal arises from the crossclaims of defendant -appellant, James R. 
Cline, and defendant-appellee, Ashley A. Lokash. Plaintiff-appellee, Premiere Settlement 
& Title, L.L.C. (“Premiere Settlement”), did not file a brief on appeal. 

PAGE 2 OF 12 

Case No. 2026-T-0029 
{¶2} Cline appeals the judgment of the Trumbull County Court of Common Pleas 
awarding summary judgment in favor of Lokash and distributing the proceeds of the sale 
of real property pursuant to the terms of the parties’ agreement. After a careful review of 
Cline’s assignment of error challenging the award of summary judgment, the record, as 
well as the pertinent law, we affirm the judgment of the trial court. 
Substantive and Procedural History 
{¶3} In March 2022, Premier Settlement, a real estate title insurance and escrow 
agency, filed a complaint against Cline and Lokash. Premier Settlement alleged it was 
retained to perform title work and escrow services for the transfer of real property located 
at 404 Bonnie Brae Avenue in Niles, Ohio (the “property”). Upon performing a title exam, 
Premiere Settlement discovered a document, entitled “Affidavit of Facts Related to 
Ownership of Real Estate,” which was filed by Lokash in the Trumbull County Recorder’s 
Office. Attached to the affidavit was an agreement between Cline and Lokash to divide 
the net proceeds in the event the property was sold. Premiere Settlement further alleged 
the affidavit was a cloud on the title; it was holding in escrow $55,568.51 from the 
proceeds of the sale; Cline had instructed Premiere Settlement not to distribute any of the 
proceeds to Lokash; and it had already distributed $15,000.00 to Cline (an amount 
Premiere Settlement believed was undisputed). 
{¶4} Premiere Settlement prayed to interplead the sum in escrow and to be 
removed from any further action in the matter. Premier Settlement further requested the 
court allow Lokash and Cline the opportunity to “set out their cause,” remove the cloud 
from the t itle, and remove the affidavit from the files of the recorder’s office. Premiere 
Settlement attached the affidavit and agreement to the complaint. 

PAGE 3 OF 12 

Case No. 2026-T-0029 
{¶5} In the affidavit, dated September 22, 2023, Lokash averred that Cline was 
the current owner of the property; she and Cline had signed and notarized the agreement; 
“the purpose of the contract was to provide for the equitable and agreed-upon distribution 
of the real estate after sale given the parties were not married at the time of the purchase 
nor during the time improvements were made to the property”; the terms of the agreement 
were clear and unambiguous; and she recorded the affidavit and agreement to p reserve 
her rights because she paid money towards the property and Cline had indicated he would 
not abide by the agreement. 
{¶6} The agreement was executed by the parties on September 27, 2021. The 
agreement set forth that Cline purchased the property though a loan guaranteed by the 
Veteran’s Administration; the parties intended to be married; Lokash was willing to use 
$40,000.00 for the purpose of upgrading the home; and the purpose of the agreement 
was to address their respective rights and obligations in the event of death or separation 
prior to their marriage. In relevant part, the parties agreed that (1) the property shall 
remain in Cline’s name; (2) Lokash “shall provide a sum not to exceed Forty Thousand 
and no/100 ($40,000) Dollars from her accounts that shall be used at the discretion of 
[Lokash] to improve the subject residence to make the home more compatible with the 
parties’ lifestyles”; and (3) Lokash will provide all the funds, sign all of the work orders, 
release funds to subcontractors, and keep a record of all receipts, disbursements, and 
transactions. The parties further agreed to the following: 
5. Upon the sale of the subject premises by [Cline] . . . the net proceeds 
shall be divided as follows: 

A. [Lokash] shall be reimbursed Forty Thousand and no/100 
($40,000.00) Dollars for the sum that she has advanced to improve 
the property. If the net proceeds from [the sale] do not equal or 
exceed said $40,000.00, then the entire net proceeds shall be 
distributed to [Lokash]. Any shortfall, or any difference between the 

PAGE 4 OF 12 

Case No. 2026-T-0029 
net proceeds and the $40,000 owed, shall be paid by [Cline] to 
[Lokash] within fourteen (14) days from the receipt of the overall net 
sales proceeds via [Cline’s] own funds, Promissory Note, Second 
Mortgage, or any combination thereof, as [Lokash] shall a gree in 
writing;1 

B. One-half of the balance of the net proceeds, if any, shall be paid 
to [Lokash]; 

C. One-half of the balance of the net proceeds, if any, shall be paid 
to [Cline]; . . . 

{¶7} Cline filed a crossclaim against Lokash, in which he alleged Lokash 
provided no sum for improvements to the property after she vacated the premises and 
their relationship ended. He further alleged that upon learning of the sale, Lokash 
maliciously and/or with reckless disregard filed the affidavit and agreement in the 
recorder’s office, placing a cloud on the title. Cline asked the court to (1) declare his 
promise to split the proceeds unenforceable because there was no consideration, (2) 
declare he is entitled to the entirety o f the net proceeds, (3) order the clerk of courts to 
release the funds from escrow, and (4) order judgment against Lokash for damages, 
including punitive damages, attorney fees, and costs. Cline attached a copy of the parties’ 
agreement to his crossclaim. 
{¶8} Lokash, in turn, filed a counter -crossclaim against Cline, raising claims of 
breach of contract, promissory estoppel, unjust enrichment, quantum meruit, and tortious 
interference. Lokash requested the court to order Cline to abide by the terms of their 
agreement, reimburse her for expenses she paid for improvements to the property, split 
the remaining proceeds, and award her costs, attorney fees, and punitive damages. 
{¶9} In October 2025, the parties filed a stipulation of facts and competing 
summary judgment motions. The parties stipulated that Cline purchased the property on 

1. Neither party argued Lokash should be reimbursed $40,000 if she spent any sum less than $40,000. 

PAGE 5 OF 12 

Case No. 2026-T-0029 
June 30, 2021. The parties were romantically involved and intended to live on the 
property together. Lokash paid $1,000.00 in earnest money, $525.00 for an appraisal, 
and $1,000.00 in closing costs, which Cline promised “at that time to reimburse the 
monies loaned by [Lokash].” In January 2020, Lokash purchased a bed for $788.38 and 
a couch for $2,196.47 that remained in Cline’s possession and that he promised to pay 
for separate and apart from their agreement. After they took possession of the property 
in July 2021, they made various improvements to the property, which Lokash paid for in 
excess of $10,000.00. In September 2021, the parties entered into the agreement. 
Between September 27, 2021, and October 23, 2021, Lokash purchased additional 
supplies for the improvements such as paint, paint supplies, molding, and yard tools that 
remained in Cline’s possession when the relationship ended and when Lokash vacated 
the premises in March 2022. Between August 2021 and March 2022, Lokash paid 
$500.00 per month in rent to Cline. In September 2022, Cline put the residence up for 
sale, and on September 26, 2023, Lokash filed the affidavit and agreement with the 
recorder’s office. On December 6, 2023, Cline sold the property to a third party. The total 
amount of proceeds in dispute is $71,897.61. Attached to the stipulations were a typed 
list of variou s payments made by Lokash, receipts of items and services Lokash 
purchased for improvements, the recorded affidavit and agreement, and closing 
documents from the sale. 
{¶10} In her motion, Lokash argued she was entitled to be reimbursed 
$17,142.00, and half of the net proceeds of $27,377.80, for a total of $44,519.80. Lokash 
argued the parties’ agreement contemplated the amounts she spent on the property both 
prior to and aft er the agreement was executed. Lokash attached to her summary 

PAGE 6 OF 12 

Case No. 2026-T-0029 
judgment motion the same documents as the stipulated exhibits in addition to text 
messages between the parties. 
{¶11} In his motion for summary judgment, Cline acknowledged Lokash should 
be reimbursed $11,035.00 for “various loans and expenditures prior to the September 27, 
2021 Agreement” and argued he is entitled to the remaining amount of the net proceeds. 
Cline further argued there was no consideration under the agreement because Lokash 
did not perform under the agreement. Cline attached no evidentiary quality materials to 
his motion. 
{¶12} In March 2026, the trial court issued a judgment on the parties’ motions, 
awarding summary judgment in favor of Lokash. After reviewing the facts and arguments 
of the parties, the court found neither of the parties were arguing the claims they had 
raised in their crossclaims; rather, they were arguing whether the agreement was 
enforceable and how much money should be distributed to each party. Thus, the central 
issue to be decided was whether Lokash had performed under the terms of the 
agreement. 
{¶13} The court reviewed there was no dispute that Lokash expended money to 
improve the property prior to the agreement. The court found this included $2,525.00 
toward the purchase of the property, $3,325.00 for flooring and carpet, $340.00 for 
Sherwin Williams, $1,185.00 for Home Depot, $266.00 for Big Lots, $81.00 for Hobby 
Lobby, $121.00 for Handyman, $208.00 for Smallwoods Carpet, and $2,196.00 for Value 
City, which included $788.38 for a bed. The court noted the parties stipulated that Lokash 
purchased “additional painting supplies, molding pieces and yard tools” after the 
agreement. Further, several of the stipulated ex hibits were receipts of purchases that 

PAGE 7 OF 12 

Case No. 2026-T-0029 
were dated after the agreement. Thus, it was clear Lokash spent money for improvement 
of the property after the agreement was executed. 
{¶14} The court further found the agreement did not state Lokash had to spend 
$40,000. Rather, it specified Lokash “shall provide a sum not to exceed Forty Thousand 
and no/100 ($40,000.00) Dollars from her accounts . . . . ” Accordingly, the court found 
that pursuant to the stipulated evidence, Lokash performed under the agreement and she 
was entitled to reimbursement for the money expended after the agreement ($1,191.34), 
as well as half of the net proceeds of the sale, an d therefore, Cline was in breach of the 
agreement. 
{¶15} As for the purchases and costs Lokash expended prior to the agreement, 
Cline stipulated and acknowledged in his motion the parties had separate, antecedent 
oral agreements for those costs. Cline believed Lokash should be reimbursed

leads.court: New Jersey Superior Court Appellate Division
leads.text:
SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO . A-2444-24 

JAMES E. HENRY, SARAH 
HENRY, and 83 MORRIS 
AVENUE, LLC, 

 Plaintiffs -Appellants, 

v. 

PLANNING BOARD OF THE 
BOROUGH OF MANASQUAN, 

 Defendant -Respondent. 
___________________________ 

 Argued September 24, 2026 – Decided October 26, 2026 

Before Judges Chase and Augostini. 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law 
Division, Monmouth County, Docket No. L -2990-23. 

James M. Turteltaub argued the cause for appellants 
(The Turteltaub Law Firm LLC, attorneys; James M. 
Turteltaub and Linda A. Turteltaub, of counsel and on 
the briefs ). 

George D. McGill argued the cause for respondent 
(McGill & Hall LLC, attorneys; George D. McGill, on 
the brief). 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court." Although it is posted on the 
internet , this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited. R. 1:36 -3. 

2 A-2444 -24 

PER CURIAM 

 Plaintiffs James E. Henry, Sarah Henry, and 83 Morris Avenue , LLC 
appeal from a January 21, 2025 order affirming defendant Planning Board of the 
Borough of Manasquan's (Board) denial of their variance application and 
dismissing their complaint in lieu of prerogative writs with prejudice. 1 We 
affirm. 
I. 
 The Henrys own residential property in Manasquan (Borough) . 83 Morris 
Avenue, LLC, a limited liability company whose only members are the Henrys , 
owns the adjacent property —a vacant lot n ext to the Henry s' home. The Robert s 
Swamp Brook, a tidal water body, runs behind the property. 
The Henrys made backyard improvements to the property , including 
building a pool, garage, patio, and retaining walls . At the time these 
improvements were made, the Department of Environmental Protection required 
certain permits to comply with wetlands and flood hazard rules . As a result, t he 

1 Plaintiffs amended notice of appeal states they are appealing from only the 
January 21, 2025 order. See R. 2:5-1(f)(2)(ii); see also W.H. Indus., Inc. v. 
Fundicao Balancins, Ltda , 397 N.J. Super. 455, 458 (App. Div. 2008). 

3 A-2444 -24 

Henrys had to raise the elevation of the ir backyard by adding three feet of fill . 
"The property needed to be filled to one foot above flood elevation," which 
caused the Henrys to install three-foot high retaining wall s on both the southeast 
and northwest property lines "to comply with the [B]orough's ordinances for 
stormwater runoff [.]" The Henrys then installed a three -foot chain link fence at 
the top of the wall . 
The Henrys wanted to replace this chain link fence with a six -foot solid 
vinyl fence, contending it was necessary to safeguard their children and keep 
their dogs corralled on the property . The Borough's zoning ordinance restricts 
fences to six feet above the "existing grade" of the property. Manasquan, N.J., 
Ordinance 2376 -22 ( Oct. 3, 2022) (containing the language at issue from 
Manasquan, N.J. , Code § 35 -7.5). Therefore, the Henrys filed a variance 
application, seeking approval to build a six-foot fence on top of the three -foot 
retaining wall for a total height of nine feet. 
 On June 20, 2023, the Board conducted a hearing on the application. James 
E. Henry testified and called two experts : a licensed professional engineer and 
a licensed project planner. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Board voted to 
deny the application. On August 1, 2023, it adopted Resolution 25 -2023, 
memorializing its decision. 

4 A-2444 -24 

On September 22, 2023, plaintiffs filed a complaint in lieu of prerogative 
writs challenging the Board 's denial of their application. On September 10, 2024, 
the court conducted a one -day trial , and after which it ordered supplemental 
briefing on whether a limited remand to the Board for interpretation of the 
municipal zoning ordinance was appropriate . On October 18 , the court remanded 
the matter to the Board for the "limited purpose [of] declar [ing] their 
interpretation of Manasquan Municipal Code § 35 -7.5," and "determin [ing] the 
meaning of the term 'existing grade' from the Code [.]" 
On December 3, 2024, the Board held a meeting at which the public, 
including the Henrys, were not permitted to participate. After some discussion, 
the Board issued Resolution 40 -2024 defining "existing grade" as "the grade of 
the land before any alterations are made to it, the original state of the grade before 
alterations, and in the subject case the grade before the construction of the 
retaining wall. " 
On January 21, 2025, the court affirmed the Board 's denial of the variance 
application and dismis sed the complaint with prejudice. Plaintiffs moved for 
reconsideration. On March 19, 2025 , the court denied reconsideration. 
On appeal, plaintiffs argue the Board's interpretation of "existing grade" 
was flawed ; the hearing on December 3, 2024 was improper ; and the variance 

5 A-2444 -24 

for the height of the fence should have been granted. They claim the Board's 
interpretation violates its own ordinance , is ambiguous, and would produce an 
absurd result. 
II. 
A. 
 "When reviewing a trial court's decision regarding the validity of a local 
board's determination, 'we are bound by the same standards as was the trial 
court.'" Jacoby v. Zoning Bd. of Adj . of Borough of Englewood , 442 N.J. Super. 
450, 462 (App. Div. 2015) (quoting Fallone Props., L .L.C. v. Bethlehem Twp. 
Plan. Bd., 369 N.J. Super. 552, 562 (App. Div. 2004)) . "We have long recognized 
that zoning boards , 'because of their peculiar knowledge of local conditions[ ,] 
must be allowed wide latitude in the exercise of delegated discretion.'" Price v. 
Himeji, LLC , 214 N.J. 263, 284 (2013) (alteration in original) (quoting Kramer 
v. Bd. of Adj. , 45 N.J. 268, 296 (1965)). A planning board's land use decisions 
are entitled to a presumption of validity . Ibid. 
Therefore, we defer to the actions of local boards , Jacoby , 442 N.J. Super. 
at 462, and reverse those decisions only if arbitrary, capricious, and 
unreasonable. Smart SMR of N.Y., Inc. v. Bor ough of Fair Lawn Bd. of Adj. , 

6 A-2444 -24 

152 N.J. 309, 327 (1998) (quoting Sica v. Bd. of Adj. , 127 N.J. 152, 166 -67 
(1992)). 
 "An appellate court reviews de novo the statutory interpretation decisions 
of a trial court ." Monarch Cmtys., LLC v. Twp. of Montville , 264 N.J. 452, 463 
(2026) (citing Cowan v. State Parole Bd. , 263 N.J. 91, 105 (2026)). When 
interpreting a statute, "[o]ur primary goal . . . 'is to discern and effectuate the 
intent of the Legislature.'" Ibid. (omission in original) (quoting Shipyard 
Assocs., LP v. City of Hoboken , 242 N.J. 23, 38-39 (2020) ) (internal quotation 
marks omitted) . "We 'consider[] the statute's plain language, ascribing to the 
words used their ordinary meaning and significance.'" Ibid. (alteration in 
original) (quoting Shipyard Assocs., LP , 242 N.J. at 38) (internal quotation marks 
omitted) . 
These well -established principles of statutory interpretation "govern the 
interpretation of a municipal ordinance []" as well. Twp. of Pennsauken v. Schad , 
160 N.J. 156, 170 (1999) (citing AMN, Inc. v. S. Brunswick Rent Leveling Bd. , 
93 N.J. 518, 524 -25 (1983) ). "[A]n ordinance should be interpreted to 'effectuate 
the legislative intent in light of the language used and the objects sought to be 
achieved.'" Ibid. (quoting Merin v. Maglaki , 126 N.J. 430, 435 (1992) ) (internal 
quotation marks omitted) . 

7 A-2444 -24 

The Henrys applied to the Board for variance relief from Ordinance § 35-
7.5, "Walls and Fences," which at the time stated : 
No wall/fence shall be erected, maintained to a height 
greater than six feet above the existing grade of the 
property, provided that the same is more than [twenty -
five] feet from any street line. No wall/fence shall be 
erected, maintained to a height greater than four feet 
within [twenty -five] feet of any street line. 

In October 2022, the ordinance was amended from a fence shall not be erected 
to a " height greater than six feet above ground level ," to a "height greater than 
six feet above the existing grade of the property." The amended ordinance's 
definition of "the existing grade of the property" is at issue in this appeal. 
 The Henrys contend the trial court erred by remanding the matter to the 
Board to interpret the term "existing grade" in Borough Ordinance § 35-7.5 and 
it should have conducted its own de novo review . Because "different 
interpretations [of existing grade] could influence [the ] court's decision," and the 
Board did not state its interpretation of this term, the court determined a remand 
for purposes of amplification was necessary. We discern no error in this 
decision. 
The trial court was tasked with determining whether the Board's denial of 
the Henrys' variance application was arbitrary, capricious, and unreasonable . In 
doing so, the court had to determine whether the Board "could reasonably have 

8 A-2444 -24 

reached its decision on the record." Cohen v. Bd. of Adj . of Rumson , 396 N.J. 
Super. 608, 615 (App. Div. 2007) (quoting Jock v. Zoning Bd. of Adj., Twp. of 
Wall, 184 N.J. 562, 597 (2005) ). Because the gravamen of the Board's decision 
rested on its interpretation of "existing grade," and "arguments [had] been raised 
[as] to what the proper interpretation of Manasquan Municipal Code § 35 -7.5 is," 
the court acted well -within its authority to issue a limited remand for the Board 
to set forth its interpretation. 
By issuing a limited remand, the court did not delegate its authority to the 
Board. Although neither party had requested a remand, the court determined the 
clarification would aid in its review of the Board's decision. After giving the 
Board an opportunity to amplify its findings, the court conducted a de novo 
review of its interpretation of "existing grade " without giving that interpretation 
any particular deference . See Reich v. Borough of Fort Lee Zoning Bd. of Adj. , 
414 N.J. Super . 483, 499 (App. Div. 2010). Indeed, by doing so, the court 
recognized the Board's specialized knowledge about its community and zoning 
ordinances. Price, 214 N.J. at 284. 
The limited remand was also proper because there were two existing grades 
on the Henrys' property: one on the internal side and one on the external side of 
the retaining wall. Thus, clarification was needed to identify which existing 

9 A-2444 -24 

grade would be used for purposes of calculating the height of the Henrys' 
proposed fence. 
The Henrys assert the Board compounded the error by its unwillingness to 
permit a hearing and testimony on the interpretation issue of "existing grade ." 
At the time of the court's remand, the record had been closed, and the purpose of 
the remand was limited to the Board's clarification on how it defined "existing 
grade." No further testimony was required for the Board to clarify its 
interpretation of this term. Under these circumstances, w e discern no error in the 
court's decision to limit the remand to the Board's amplification of the term 
"existing grade " without further testimony or evidence. 
B. 
 The Board memorialized its interpretation of the term existing grade in 
Resolution 40 -2024, stating the phrase means "the grade of the land before any 
alterations are made to it , the original state of the grade before alterations, and in 
the subject case the grade before the construction of the retaining wall." 
The Henrys argue the court erred by not interpreting the ordinance's plain , 
unambiguous language to mean the grade of the land as it presently exists . They 
assert this interpretation conflicts with Borough Ordinance § 35-3(a), "Word 
Usage," which provides "[w]ords used in the present tense include the future 

10 A-2444 -24 

tense." The Henrys further contend the court "rubberstamped" the Bo

NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

 SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO. A-0491-25 

JORGE FELICIANO, 

Appellant, 

v. 

BOARD OF REVIEW, 
DEPARTMENT OF LABOR 
AND WORKFORCE 
DEVELOPMENT, and 
KITCHENALL, LLC, 

Respondents. 

Argued September 22, 2026 – Decided October 26, 2026. 

Before Judges Gooden Brown, Vanek and Bergman. 

On appeal from the Board of Review, Division of 
Unemployment, Department of Labor and Workforce 
Development, Docket No. 372626. 

Sarah Hymowitz argued the cause for appellant (Legal 
Services of New Jersey, attorneys; Sarah Hymowitz, on 
the briefs). 

Kevin K.O. Sangster, Deputy Attorney General, argued 
the cause for respondent Board of Review, Department 
of Labor and Workforce Development (Jennifer 
Davenport, Attorney General, attorney; Sookie Bae -
Park, Assistant Attorney General, of counsel; Kevin 
K.O. Sangster, on the briefs). 
APPROVED FOR PUBLICATION 

October 26, 2026 

APPELLATE DIVISION 

 A-0491 -25 
2 
Kevin J. Stawicki argued the cause for respondent 
Kitchenall, LLC (Genova Burns LLC, attorneys; Kevin 
J. Stawicki, on the brief). 

Adam L. Schorr argued the cause for amicus curiae 
National Employment Lawyers Association – New 
Jersey (Schorr Law, PC, attorneys; Adam L. Schorr, of 
counsel and on the brief). 

The opinion of the court was delivered by 

BERGMAN, J.A.D. 
Petitioner Jorge Feliciano appeals from the August 27, 2025 final decision 
of the Board of Review , Department of Labor and Workforce Development 
(Board) affirming the Department of Labor Appeal Tribunal 's (Tribunal) 
dismissal of his appeal from an initial unemployment determination as untimely. 
The Tribunal concluded petitioner 's appeal was barred by N.J.S.A. 43:21 -6(b)(1) 
solely because it was filed twenty-two days after the mailing date of the initial 
determination , one day beyond the twenty -one-day statutory period set forth in 
the statute . The Board affirmed. 
Having considered the arguments in light of the record and the governing 
legal principles, we vacate the Board 's decision and remand for further 
proceedings consistent with this opinion . We hold, a lthough the 2022 
amendment to N.J.S.A. 43:21 -6(b)(1) enlarged the appeal filing period for 
claimants from ten days to twenty -one days after mailing, neither the 
amendment 's plain langua ge nor its legislative history demonstrate the 

 A-0491 -25 
3 
legislature intended to displace the due process "good cause " principles 
recognized by the Court in Rivera v. Board of Review , 127 N.J. 578 (1992), or 
to eliminate consideration of whether a late filing resulted from circumstances 
beyond the petitioner 's control. Here, although the Tribunal permitted and 
received testimony concerning petitioner 's limited English proficiency and his 
efforts to secure translation assistance as reasons for his late filing , neither the 
tribunal nor the Board rendered dispositive findings concerning petitioner 's 
request to accept his late appeal. Because the agency decisions did not 
determine whether petitioner established good cause for the one -day filing delay 
on the merits , we vacate the Board's final agency decision and remand for 
consider ation as to whether petitioner demonstrated "good cause " for his late 
filing, and if so, direct the agency to decide petitioner 's appeal on its merits. 
I. 
We recite the facts and procedural history relevant to our opinion from the 
administrative record. On April 7, 2024, petitioner filed a claim for 
unemployment benefits with the New Jersey Department of Labor (NJDOL). 
On May 7, 2024, the NJDOL mailed a Notice of Determination to petitioner , 
holding him ineligible for benefits because he had insufficient base weeks or 
earnings to establish a valid claim. Petitioner , wh o claimed his primary 
language is Spanish and has limited English proficiency, received the 

 A-0491 -25 
4 
determination but claimed he did not understand its contents. He asserts within 
five to seven days of receiving the notice, he sought translation assistance at his 
local Board of Social Services office, which then referred him to Legal Services 
of New Jersey (LSNJ) for further assistance . Petitioner contacted LSNJ, and on 
May 29, 2024, with their assistance, filed an appeal of the initial determination. 
The appeal was filed twenty -two days after the date the determination was 
mailed, making it one day late under the statutory twenty -one-day deadline set 
forth in N.J.S.A. 43:21 -6(b)(1). 
On January 24, 2025, the Tribunal conducted a telephonic hearing, at 
which petitioner appeared with counsel and testified regarding both the 
timeliness of his appeal and the circumstances of his termination from 
employment. During the hearing, petitioner explained he did not understand the 
determination due to the language barrier and described the steps he took to seek 
assistance and to file his appeal. Stephen Rahavy, the president of Kitchenall, 
LLC (Kitchenall) , also participated in the hearing and testified regarding the 
reasons for petitioner 's termination from employment. 
Rahavy recounted Scott Stevens, the director of Warehouse Operations, 
terminated petitioner because he smelled alcohol on petitioner 's breath and 
petitioner admitted to having a few beers during lunch. Rahavy testified 
although he was unsure whether there was a written company policy prohibiting 

 A-0491 -25 
5 
alcohol consumption during work hours , he considered it to be "common sense, " 
but admitted petitioner had not received prior warnings. Bulinski, a partner at 
the company, also testified he smelled alcohol on petitioner 's breath, reported it 
to Stevens, and later spoke to petitioner by phone after his discharge, during 
which petitioner allegedly acknowledged drinking. Petitioner denied drinking 
on the job or being told he was discharged for that reason, asserting instead he 
was simply told he was no longer needed. He also denied violating any company 
policies or receiving prior warnings. 
Following the hearing, the Tribunal issued a written decision on January 
24, 2025, dismissing petitioner 's appeal as untimely, finding the appeal was not 
filed within the time period as required by N.J.S.A. 43:21 -6(b)(1) . The 
Tribunal 's findings of fact were limited to two sentences: "The Deputy mailed 
a determination to the appellant 's address of record on May 7, 2024. Th e 
claimant filed an appeal on May 29, 2024. " The decision did not mention 
petitioner 's testimony about his limited English proficiency, his efforts to obtain 
translation assistance, or the sequence of events leading to the one -day delay. 
Nor did it make any finding concerning good cause. 
Petitioner appealed the dismissal to the Board of Review, arguing his late 
filing was due to circumstances beyond his control, specifically his limited 
English proficiency and the need to seek translation assistance. On August 27, 

 A-0491 -25 
6 
2025, the Board of Review issued a decision affirming the Tribunal 's dismissal . 
The Board 's decision stated "[s]ince the appellant was given a full and impartial 
hearing and a complete opportunity to offer any and all evidence, there is no 
valid ground for a further hearing. " It also stated: "On the basis of the record 
below, we agree with the decision reached. " The Board did not discuss 
claimant 's language -related explanation for the late filing and, like the Tribunal, 
did not address whether petitioner had established good cause. 
Petitioner appeale d, and we granted the National Employment Lawyers 
Association 's motion to appear as Amicus Curiae. On appeal, petitioner

"good cause " exceptions violates constitutional guarantees of equal protection 
because there is no rational basis for requiring notice for employers but not

actual receipt of initial determinations and authorizing "good cause " exceptions 

 A-0491 -25 
7

recognized "good cause " exceptions for late appeals where the delay was due to

II. 
"We review a decision made by an administrative agency entrusted to 
apply and enforce a statutory scheme under an enhanced deferential standard. " 
E. Bay Drywall, LLC v. Dep 't of Lab. & Workforce Dev. , 251 N.J. 477, 493 
(2022). Accordingly, "we will disturb an agency 's adjudicatory decision only 
upon a finding the decision is 'arbitrary, capricious or unreasonable, ' or is

Sullivan v. Bd. of Rev., Dep 't of Lab. , 471 N.J. Super. 147, 155 -56 (App. Div. 
2022) (quoting Henry v. Rahway State Prison , 81 N.J. 571, 579 -80 (1980)). The

Parsells v. Bd. of Educ. of Somerville , 472 N.J. Super. 369, 376 (App. Div.

In determining whether an agency 's action is arbitrary, capricious, or 
unreasonable, we must examine: 
(1) [W]hether the agency 's action violates express or 
implied legislative policies, that is, did the agency 
follow the law;

8 
(2) whether the record contains substantial evidence to

action; and 

(3) whether in applying the legislative policies to the 
facts, the agency clearly erred in reaching a conclusion 
that could not reasonably have been made on a showing 
of the relevant factors. 

[Sullivan , 471 N.J. Super. at 156 (alteration in original) 
(quoting In re Carter , 191 N.J. 474, 482 -83 (2007)).] 

N.J.A.C. 12:20 -3.1(i) , which was in effect at the time of petitioner 's appeal 
of the initi al denial remains in effect , and provides: 
A late appeal shall be considered on its merits if it is

In the United States Court of Federal Claims
 FOR PUBLICATION

 No. 25-453L
 (Filed: October 23, 2026)

 )
 M. L. ONNA BARRY, et al., )
 )
 Plaintiffs, )
 )
 v. )
 )
 UNITED STATES, )
 )
 Defendant. )
 )

Steven M. Wald, Stewart, Wald & Smith, LLC, St. Louis, Missouri, for plaintiffs.
With him on the briefs were Michael J. Smith and Allison P. Bettlach (argued),
Stewart, Wald & Smith, LLC, St. Louis, Missouri; and Thomas S. Stewart and
Reed W. Ripley, Stewart, Wald & Smith, LLC, Prairie Village, KS.

Kenneth G. Long (argued), Senior Attorney, Environmental Enforcement Section,
Environment & Natural Resources Division, U.S. Department of Justice,
Washington, DC, for defendant. With him on the briefs was Adam R. F. Gustafson,
Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General, U.S. Department of Justice,
Washington, DC.

 OPINION AND ORDER1
BONILLA, Judge.

 Landowners in Henderson and Transylvania counties, North Carolina, seek
just compensation under the Fifth Amendment for the government’s alleged taking
of their property stemming from the conversion of a rail corridor into a public linear
park under the National Trail Systems Act (Trails Act), 16 U.S.C. §§ 1241–51.
Pending before the Court are cross-motions for summary judgment addressing
liability. The central question is whether plaintiffs owned a cognizable property

1 This case was transferred to the undersigned for adjudication on September 2, 2026, pursuant to

Rule 40.1(b) of the Rules of the United States Court of Federal Claims (RCFC).
 interest in the contested land on the date of the alleged taking. The short answer is
no. Accordingly, plaintiffs’ motion is denied, and defendant’s cross-motion is granted.

 BACKGROUND

 The critical facts of this case date back to the late nineteenth century. In early
1891, the North Carolina General Assembly chartered the Hendersonville and
Brevard Railway, Telegraph and Telephone Company (HBR).2 The shortline railroad
and communications company acquired the assets of the abandoned French Broad
Valley Railroad Company and its name from the intended 21.6-mile route between
Hendersonville and Brevard.3 To secure the land on which to build the rail line
(rail corridor), HBR executed a series of deeds between 1894 and 1895 (source deeds),
nine of which are at issue here.4 After HBR went bankrupt in 1897, the railroad’s
assets, including the rail corridor, were purchased at auction by J. Frances Hayes for
$95,000, passed to the Toxaway Company, and reorganized as the Transylvania
Railroad Company. In the early 1900s, the Southern Railway purchased a controlling
interest in the railroad, absorbing the Transylvania Railroad Company in 1906.5 In
1982, Southern Railway merged with the Norfolk and Western Railway to form the
Norfolk Southern Railway Company (NSRC). See Norfolk S. Corp.–Control–Norfolk
& W. Ry. Co. and S. Ry. Co., 366 I.C.C. 173 (1982). Watco Companies, LLC acquired
the railroad assets in June 2014 and formed the Blue Ridge Southern Railroad
(Blue Ridge). See 79 Fed. Reg. 40204 (July 11, 2014); ECF 15-6 (Quitclaim Deed 1596-
628 from NSRC to Blue Ridge (July 25, 2014)).

 On October 26, 2020, Blue Ridge and Ecusta Rails2Trails LLC (Ecusta) signed
an Interim Trail Use/Railbanking Purchase Agreement, through which Blue Ridge
agreed to sell its rights and interest in, and title to, the inactive 19.1-mile rail corridor

2 An Act to Incorporate the Hendersonville and Brevard Railway, Telegraph and Telephone Company,

ch. 360, 1891 N.C. Sess. Laws 431, available at ECF 15-1 at 3–6.
3 Jerry Ledford, A Brief History of the Railroad from Hendersonville to Lake Toxaway, Etowa NC

Heritage, available at https://perma.cc/U6HL-ELG9.
4 HBR’s charter authorized the railroad:

 to acquire, hold, sell and convey real and personal property to such an extent as to
 them may seem proper, and take title thereto in the name of the corporation, and
 convey the same through their officers in the same way that other corporations are
 now by law authorized to convey real estate : Provided, that the said corporation shall
 not at any time hold more than ten thousand acres of land.
1891 N.C. Sess. Laws 431 § 2.
5 See In Transylvania County (1861–1911), The Transylvania Heritage Museum, available at

https://perma.cc/R9A7-VGE9; Ledford, supra note 3; John Leynes, Hendersonville & Brevard Railroad
Telegraph & Telephone Co., Ry. & Locomotive Hist. Soc’y, Inc. (Southeast Chapter), no. 114, Aug. 2009,
at 2, available at https://perma.cc/H9GV-3LEN.

 2
 to Ecusta pursuant to the Trails Act for $7.76 million.6 Blue Ridge initiated a formal
exemption proceeding on April 7, 2021, filing a Verified Notice of Exemption with the
Surface Transportation Board (STB) pursuant to 49 C.F.R. § 1152.50. While the April
7, 2021 notice nominally sought authority to abandon the 19.1-mile rail corridor, Blue
Ridge made clear that it was “seeking abandonment authorization to render the Line
eligible for an interim trail[] use pursuant to 16 U.S.C. §1247(d). . . . [Blue Ridge] does
not intend to consummate abandonment of the line.” ECF 13-2 at 6; accord id. at 5
(“[Blue Ridge] anticipates that abandonment authorization will facilitate interim use
of the Line as a public recreational trail, consistent with 16 U.S.C. § 1247(d).”). The
STB granted the exemption on April 27, 2021, with an effective date of May 27, 2021.
Consistent with Blue Ridge’s April 7, 2021 representation, Blue Ridge and Ecusta
filed a Joint Petition for Interim Trail Use and Notification of Trail Use/Railbanking
Agreement on June 16, 2021.7 The STB issued the requested Notice of Interim Trail
Use or Abandonment (NITU) on June 29, 2021. The same day, Blue Ridge and Ecusta
notified the STB that they had reached a Trail Use Agreement. Blue Ridge then
executed a special warranty deed on August 12, 2021, transferring the rail corridor
to Ecusta “in fee simple.” ECF 15-8 at 3.

 On March 11, 2025, seven residents and a local volunteer fire department of
Henderson and Transylvania counties filed this Fifth Amendment takings action.8
The parties agree the remaining plaintiffs owned land adjacent to the rail corridor on
June 29, 2021, when the STB issued the NITU. The conflict lies in the property
interest HBR acquired from the predecessors-in-title to the plaintiffs 132 years ago:

 Plaintiff Source Deed Date ECF 15
 M. L. Onna Barry J. W. & Onnie Morgan Aug. 22, 1894 Ex. 9
 Sherri Leigh Bethel J. H. Ripley Oct. 22, 1894 Ex. 10
 Hugh F. & C. A. Johnson Aug. 23, 1894 Ex. 11
 M. J. & C. B. Allen Aug. 23, 1894 Ex. 12
 Kimberly Collins Fielding Cantrell Aug. 23, 1894 Ex. 13
 Wm. N. & E. C. Corn Aug. 23, 1894 Ex. 14
 Jeffrey Hart Butler & S. E. Capps Aug. 23, 1894 Ex. 15
 Kevin Landrum J. H. Ripley Oct. 22, 1894 Ex. 10

6 Ecusta is “a subsidiary of Conserving Carolina, . . . formed to acquire the railbanked corridor with

the support of local and state grants and private donors.” Our History, Friends of the Ecusta Trail,
available at https://perma.cc/N6JF-B3RU. The community-based effort “to repurpose the abandoned
19+ mile [railway] spur . . . and transform it into a multi-use greenway” dates to 2009. Id.
7 The STB’s April 27, 2021 grant of abandonment exemption included a May 7, 2021 deadline for filing

for interim trail use/rail banking requests. ECF 13-3 at 3. The STB excused Blue Ridge and Ecusta’s
late filing for good cause. Compare ECF 13-4 at 3 (“Good Cause for Late-Filed Request”), with
ECF 13-1 at 2 (issuing Notice of Interim Trail Use or Abandonment notwithstanding untimely
request).
8 The original plaintiffs included Henderson County residents M. L. Onna Barry, Sherri Leigh Bethel,

Kimberly Collins, Jeffrey Hart, Kevin Landrum, and James Quinn; Transylvania County resident
Ronald Lyday; and the Little River Volunteer Fire Department, located in Transylvania County. On
April 1, 2026, Messrs. Quinn and Lyday voluntarily dismissed their claims without prejudice.

 3
  Little River Volunteer G. W. & Mattie Allison Nov. 2, 1894 Ex. 16
 Fire Department W. M. & S. M. Allison Nov. 2, 1894 Ex. 17

 If, as the government contends, HBR acquired the contested land in fee simple
under the 1894 source deeds, plaintiffs would not have a cognizable property interest
in the contested rail corridor. Conversely, if as plaintiffs maintain, HBR acquired
only a right-of-way easement for the limited purpose of operating the planned
railroad—by deed or through prescriptive easement—the STB’s June 29, 2021
facilitation of the rail-to-trail conversion could constitute a permanent taking of
plaintiffs’ properties. Cf. Barron v. United States, __ F.4th __, No. 25-1179, 2026 WL
3160493, at *2 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 22, 2026) (“If [the deeds] conveyed an interest in fee
simple, there was no reversionary interest left to the Landowners’ predecessors-in-
interest, [and] no taking occurred . . . . Conversely, if they conveyed only an easement
for railroad use, there was a reversionary interest, and . . . the Claims Court [must]
determine the nature and status of the easement.” (citations omitted)). Plaintiffs
seek to recover the fair market value of their extinguished property rights.

 DISCUSSION
 I. Standard of Review

 Summary judgment is appropriate “if the movant shows that there is no
genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a
matter of law.” RCFC 56(a). A genuine dispute exists where a reasonable factfinder
“could return a verdict for the nonmoving party.” Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc.,
477 U.S. 242, 248 (1986). Material facts, in turn, are those “that might affect the
outcome of the suit.” Id. In deciding motions for summary judgment, the Court must
draw all inferences in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party, evaluating
each motion on its own merits. Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp.,
475 U.S. 574, 587–88 (1986) (quoting United States v. Diebold, Inc., 369 U.S. 654, 655
(1962)); Mingus Constructors, Inc. v. United States, 812 F.2d 1387, 1391 (Fed. Cir.
1987).

 The moving party bears the initial burden to demonstrate the absence of any
genuine issue of material fact. See Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 323 (1986).
That burden can be met by showing “there is an absence of evidence to support the
nonmoving party’s case.” Dairyland Power Coop. v. United States, 16 F.3d 1197, 1202
(Fed. Cir. 1994) (citing Celotex, 477 U.S. at 325). “Once the moving party has satisfied
its initial burden, the opposing party must establish a genuine issue of material fact
and cannot rest on mere allegations, but must present actual evidence.” Crown
Operations Int’l, Ltd. v. Solutia Inc., 289 F.3d 1367, 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2002) (citing
Anderson, 477 U.S. at 248). Summary judgment is warranted when “the record taken
as a whole could not lead a rational trier of fact to find for the non-moving party.”
Matsushita, 475 U.S. at 587.

 4
  II. Fifth Amendment Taking

 A compensable Fifth Amendment claim requires a cognizable interest in the
property allegedly taken. Palmyra Pac. Seafoods, LLC v. United States, 561 F.3d
1361, 1364 (Fed. Cir. 2009) (citing Phillips v. Wash. Legal Found., 524 U.S. 156, 164
(1998)). In Trails Act cases, the initial inquiry is whether the railroad acquired
fee simple title in the land underlying the contested rail corridor or merely secured a
railway easement over the owner’s burdened freehold estate. Preseault v. United
States, 100 F.3d 1525, 1533–34 (Fed. Cir. 1996) (en banc). Where the railroad secured
only right-of-way easements, two follow-on questions remain:

 [W]ere the terms of the easements limited to use for railroad purposes,
 or did they include future use as public recreational trails; and . . . even
 if the grants of the [r]ailroad’s easements were broad enough to
 encompass recreational trails, had these easements terminated prior to
 the alleged taking so that the property owners at that time held fee
 simples unencumbered by the easements[?]

Id. at 1533. Property rights in rails-to-trails cases ar

USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 1 of 16

 PUBLISHED

 UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
 FOR THE FOURTH CIRCUIT

 No. 25-1797

 SOUTH CAROLINA COASTAL CONSERVATION LEAGUE; CHARLESTON
 WATERKEEPER; SOUTH CAROLINA WILDLIFE FEDERATION,

 Plaintiffs - Appellants,

 v.

 UNITED STATES ARMY CORPS OF ENGINEERS, Charleston District;
 LIEUTENANT GENERAL WILLIAM H. GRAHAM, JR., in his official capacity
 as Chief of Engineers; UNITED STATES ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION
 AGENCY; LEE M. ZELDIN, in his official capacity as Administrator of the U.S.
 Environmental Protection Agency; UNITED STATES FISH AND WILDLIFE
 SERVICE; LIEUTENANT COLONEL TODD MAINWARING, in his official
 capacity as Commander of the Charleston District; DANIEL P. DRISCOLL, in his
 official capacity as Secretary of the U.S. Army; DOUG BURGUM, in his official
 capacity as Secretary of the United States Department of the Interior,

 Defendants - Appellees,

 and

 TRACT 1 TIMBER, LLC; SEVEN STICKS, LLC; TRACT 7, LLC; CAINHOY
 LAND AND TIMBER, LLC,

 Intervenors/Defendants - Appellees.

 Appeal from the United States District Court for the District of South Carolina, at
 Charleston. Richard Mark Gergel, District Judge. (2:22-cv-02727-RMG)

 Argued: September 10, 2026 Decided: October 23, 2026
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 2 of 16

 Before AGEE, THACKER, and BERNER, Circuit Judges.

 Affirmed by published opinion. Judge Thacker wrote the opinion in which Judge Agee
 and Judge Berner joined.

 ARGUED: Catherine Moore Wannamaker, SOUTHERN ENVIRONMENTAL LAW
 CENTER, Charleston, South Carolina, for Appellants. Jacob David Ecker, UNITED
 STATES DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE, Washington, D.C.; Michael Rhett DeHart,
 ADAMS & REESE LLP, Charleston, South Carolina, for Appellees. ON BRIEF:
 Christopher, K. DeScherer, Emily C. Wyche, SOUTHERN ENVIRONMENTAL LAW
 CENTER, Charleston, South Carolina, for Appellants. Adam R.F. Gustafson, Principal
 Deputy Assistant Attorney General, Rebecca Jaffe, Kristen Sarna, Environment and
 Natural Resources Division, UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,
 Washington, D.C., for Federal Appellees.

 2
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 3 of 16

 THACKER, Circuit Judge:

 The United States Army Corps of Engineers (the “Corps”) issued a permit pursuant

 to Section 404 of the Clean Water Act (“CWA”) for the development of the Cainhoy

 Plantation (“Cainhoy”), a residential and commercial development in Charleston, South

 Carolina, after determining the proposed project was the least environmentally damaging

 practicable alternative (“LEDPA”). South Carolina Coastal Conservation League,

 Charleston Waterkeeper, and South Carolina Wildlife Federation (collectively,

 “Appellants”) allege the Corps’ LEDPA determination was arbitrary and capricious

 because the Corps did not consider on-site alternatives affecting less than the proposed

 181.5 acres of wetlands impact. The district court granted summary judgment in favor of

 the Corps.

 Because we conclude the Corps conducted a thorough and reasoned analysis and

 did not act in an arbitrary or capricious manner, we affirm the district court.

 I.

 Tract 1 Timber, LLC, Seven Sticks, LLC, Tract 7, LLC, and Cainhoy Land and

 Timber, LLC (collectively, “Intervenors”) own approximately 16,000 acres of private land

 in Berkeley County, South Carolina. Cainhoy, the property at issue in this appeal,

 comprises 9,076 acres of the total acreage. Intervenors have used Cainhoy as a pine tree

 timber farm for the last 90 years. In 1996, the city of Charleston, South Carolina annexed

 Cainhoy into the city limits and sought to have Intervenors develop Cainhoy to allow for

 growth in the city.

 3
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 4 of 16

 Today, Cainhoy’s surrounding areas have substantially transformed into residential

 and industrial development. Cainhoy is currently zoned as a Planned Unit Development

 (“PUD”), defined as consisting of “a tract or tracts of land under unified control, planned

 and developed as a whole in a single development stage or phased series of development

 stages according to an approved PUD Master Plan.” J.A. 1024–25. 1

 Though Cainhoy totals over 9,000 acres, including over 2,500 acres of wetlands, the

 proposed Cainhoy development will develop only 3,906 acres, including 181.5 acres of

 wetlands. The remaining acres are to be placed in conservation easements and/or

 restrictive covenants to permanently protect the property. Cainhoy is planned to be a mixed

 use commercial and residential development, eventually containing residences, schools,

 medical and assisted living facilities, and other community services.

 In order to accomplish the goal of developing Cainhoy, Intervenors began applying

 for the required permits in 2012, including a CWA Section 404 permit. A Section 404

 permit was required because the development would affect wetlands on the property. An

 early design of the project called for 1,820.1 acres of wetlands impact. But, “[t]hrough the

 avoidance and minimization process, [Intervenors] expressed [a] desire for a conservation

 minded, environmentally sensitive” development. J.A. 919. To accomplish this, the Corps

 and Intervenors focused on only affecting wetlands necessary for road crossings, feasible

 lot development, and essential storm water ponds. As a result, the wetlands impact was

 1
 Citations to the “J.A.” refer to the Joint Appendix filed by the parties in this appeal.

 4
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 5 of 16

 reduced to 187.9 acres. And, in 2022, Intervenors and the Corps further decreased the

 wetlands impact to 181.5 acres.

 In March 2018, pursuant to Section 404 of the CWA, the Corps provided initial

 notice to the public and invited comments regarding the proposed project. The Corps

 received a significant number of comments and addressed each one, spanning 84 pages, in

 an Environment Assessment (the “EA”). After considering all of the public comments, the

 Corps detailed its decision and findings in the EA, which it issued in 2022.

 The Corps conducted an extensive EA, which included a review of the proposed

 plan, 14 alternative plans, and a no action option. The no action option entailed denying

 Intervenors’ permit and leaving Cainhoy open for future, independent development. To

 help guide its analysis of the alternatives, the Corps first determined the project’s overall

 purpose. The Corps described the project’s purpose as a development plan “to construct a

 mixed use development to include residential, commercial, educational, office and

 government facilities with access to major traffic arteries that has the demographic support,

 zoning, infrastructure and access to schools and hospitals to help meet the needs of the

 growing Charleston, South Carolina metropolitan area.” J.A. 931.

 The Corps’ nine off-site alternative plans were located in the Charleston area.

 Consistent with the purpose of the project, the Corps considered whether each alterative

 satisfied certain criteria in determining whether an off-site alternative was practicable. In

 particular, the Corps evaluated whether the off-site alternatives

 • were located within 50 miles of Charleston, South Carolina;
 • had a commute time of 45 minutes or less;

 5
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 6 of 16

 • contained a minimum of 7,500 acres with 5,000 acres developable uplands 2;
 • were within a ten mile radius of an interstate or four lane major highway;
 • were able to be developed and not currently part of a planned development;
 • had access to utilities infrastructure (available and practicable);
 • were appropriately zoned for mixed-use development.

 Each of the nine off-site alternatives was determined to be impracticable by the Corps

 because none satisfied the required criteria.

 The Corps also considered four on-site alternatives but determined each would have

 a greater impact on wetlands than the proposed plan. Finally, the Corps considered a plan

 proposed by Appellants -- the “Dover plan.” 3 The Dover plan included four versions,

 ranging from no wetlands impact to 13.2 acres of wetlands impact. But no version of the

 Dover plan accounted for the entire Cainhoy property -- roughly 8,000 acres would be left

 undeveloped under each iteration. The Corps concluded this would likely contribute

 significantly to future wetlands impacts because of the possibility of future development

 of the remaining acreage, and because no version contained preservation or conservation

 efforts for the undeveloped land. Moreover, the Corps determined that the Dover plan was

 a “distinctly different project” and therefore did not comply with the project’s overall

 purpose. J.A. 1052.

 2
 Uplands are areas of “high land especially at some distance from the sea.” Upland,
 Merriam-Webster, https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/upland
 [https://perma.cc/7VWP-5CP7] (last visited Oct. 6, 2026).
 3
 Appellants’ proposed plan was referred to as the Dover plan because it was
 prepared by Dover, Kohl, and Partners, an urban planning firm.

 6
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 7 of 16

 Lastly, the Corps considered a no action plan. Under a no action plan, Intervenors’

 permit would be denied, leaving Cainhoy open to smaller parcel development plans. The

 Corps concluded that the no action plan would potentially impact more wetlands, and

 prevent the property from receiving the benefit of Intervenors’ “comprehensive approach

 to a compensatory mitigation plan that protects the most ecologically valuable on-site

 wetlands.” J.A. 1051.

 After a full analysis, the Corps determined that Intervenors’ proposed project was

 the LEDPA and issued a Section 404 permit for it in May 2022. Appellants challenged the

 2022 permit, naming the Corps, the Fish and Wildlife Service, and the Environmental

 Protection Agency (the “EPA”) as defendants. Appellants argued that the Corps acted

 arbitrarily and capriciously in issuing the permit, and raised their challenges pursuant to

 the CWA citizen suit provision and the Administrative Procedure Act (the “APA”).

 The Corps moved to dismiss the CWA citizen suit provision claim, arguing the

 court’s jurisdiction arose pursuant to the APA instead. But the district court denied the

 motion and held that its subject matter jurisdiction derived from the citizen suit provision

 of the CWA. Therefore, the court dismissed the APA claim. In so holding, the district

 court relied on National Wildlife Federation v. Hanson, 859 F.2d 313 (4th Cir. 1988).

 Subsequently, the parties filed cross motions for summary judgment, and the district

 court granted summary judgment in favor of the Corps and Intervenors, dismissing the case

 with prejudice. The district court reaffirmed its conclusion that jurisdiction lay pursuant

 to the CWA, not the APA. And on the merits, the district court held that the Corps’ actions

 7
 USCA4 Appeal: 25-1797 Doc: 75 Filed: 10/23/2026 Pg: 8 of 16

 were neither arbitrary nor capricious because it conducted an extensive analysis of

 numerous alternatives in arriving at its LEDPA determination.

 Appellants timely appealed, arguing that the district court erred in concluding that

 the Corps’ LEDPA determination was not arbitrary or capricious.

 II.

 “We review the district court’s legal conclusions regarding its own subject matter

 jurisdiction de novo.” Flame S.A. v. Freight Bulk Pte. Ltd., 762 F.3d 352, 356 (4th Cir.

 2014) (internal citation omitted). “Our review of a district court’s grant of summary

 judgment is de novo.” Deque Sys. Inc. v. Browserstack, Inc., 177 F.4th 585, 598 (4th Cir.

 2026). “Summary judgment is appropriate when there is no genuine issue of material fact

 and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Sigley v. ND Fairmont

 LLC, 129 F.4th
